Fuzz testing has been gaining ground recently with substantial e orts devoted to the area. Typically, fuzzers take a set of seed inputs and leverage random mutations to continually improve the inputs with respect to a cost, e.g. program code coverage, to discover vulnerabilities or bugs. Following this methodology, fuzzers are very good at generating unstructured inputs that achieve high coverage. However fuzzers are less e ective when the inputs are structured, say they conform to an input grammar. Due to the nature of random mutations, the overwhelming abundance of inputs generated by this common fuzzing practice often adversely hinders the effectiveness and efficiency of fuzzers on grammar-aware applications. The problem of testing becomes even harder, when the goal is not only to achieve increased code coverage, but also to nd complex vulnerabilities related to other cost measures, say high resource consumption in an application.
          We propose Saffron an adaptive grammar-based fuzzing approach to effectively and efficiently generate inputs that expose expensive executions in programs. Saffron takes as input a user-provided grammar, which describes the input space of the program under analysis, and uses it to generate test inputs. Saffron assumes that the grammar description is approximate since precisely describing the input program space is often difficult as a program may accept unintended inputs due to e.g., errors in parsing. Yet these inputs may reveal worst-case complexity vulnerabilities. The novelty of Saffron is then twofold: (1) Given the user-provided grammar, Saffron attempts to discover whether the program accepts unexpected inputs outside of the provided grammar, and if so, it repairs the grammar via grammar mutations. The repaired grammar serves as a speci cation of the actual inputs accepted by the application. (2) Based on the re ned grammar, it generates concrete test inputs. It starts by treating every production rule in the grammar with equal probability of being used for generating concrete inputs. It then adaptively re nes the probabilities along the way by increasing the probabilities for rules that have been used to generate inputs that improve a cost, e.g., code coverage or arbitrary user-de ned cost. Evaluation results show that Saffron signi cantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

result.paraphrase:
Fuzz testing has recently been gaining traction, with considerable effort devoted to the area. In general, fuzzers begin with seed inputs and apply random mutations to steadily improve those inputs according to a cost metric, such as program code coverage, in order to uncover bugs or vulnerabilities. Using this approach, fuzzers are well suited to producing unstructured inputs that obtain high coverage. However, they are less effective for structured inputs, such as those that follow an input grammar. Because random mutations are used, the large number of inputs produced by this common fuzzing method often hurts the effectiveness and efficiency of fuzzers on grammar-aware applications. Testing becomes even more difficult when the objective is not only higher code coverage, but also the discovery of complex vulnerabilities tied to other cost measures, such as excessive resource consumption in an application.

We present Saffron, an adaptive grammar-based fuzzing approach for efficiently and effectively generating inputs that reveal expensive program executions. Saffron accepts a user-provided grammar describing the program’s input space and uses it to generate test cases. It assumes this grammar is approximate, since precisely specifying the program’s input space is often hard and programs may accept unintended inputs due to, for example, parsing errors. Such inputs, however, may expose worst-case complexity vulnerabilities. Saffron’s novelty is twofold: first, given the user grammar, it tries to determine whether the program accepts unexpected inputs outside that grammar and, if so, repairs the grammar through grammar mutations. The repaired grammar then acts as a specification of the actual inputs accepted by the application. Second, using the refined grammar, it generates concrete test inputs. Initially, every production rule in the grammar is treated as equally likely to be used when generating concrete inputs. It then adapts these probabilities over time, increasing the likelihood of rules that have produced inputs improving a cost, such as code coverage or any user-defined cost. Experimental results show that Saffron substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
